url: /agents.md
---
# Using it with an AI agent.

The tool prints its own guidance, so any agent that can run `npx` can learn to use it. If the tool is installed globally, the agent can run `automatica11y guide skill` instead of `npx automatica11y@latest guide skill`:

```bash
npx automatica11y@latest guide            # where to start (the AGENTS.md file)
npx automatica11y@latest guide skill      # the core steps: check, build the command, run it
npx automatica11y@latest guide setup      # what to do for each doctor state (browser, Node)
npx automatica11y@latest guide targets    # local pages, Storybooks, npm packages, and grouping
npx automatica11y@latest guide site       # crawling a site, sitemaps, and authentication
npx automatica11y@latest guide fixtures   # how to write the fixtures an npm package needs
npx automatica11y@latest guide reporting  # how to write the report from the results
```

The core steps are small, and they tell the agent which other topic to read, only when the request needs it. That keeps the agent's context free for the work. For setup, the agent runs `doctor --json`, which names the environment's state, so the agent follows the tool's diagnosis instead of interpreting prose.

The guidance ships with the tool, so it always matches the version you run. Tell your agent to run `npx automatica11y@latest guide` and follow it, then ask for things like "How accessible is Radix Dialog?" or "Compare the accessibility of React Aria and Headless UI." The agent needs to run shell commands and read and write files. Nothing here is tied to one agent.

Shell networking can be restricted separately from web search or browser access. If npm can't reach the registry, the agent can request network permission for the exact guide command where the execution environment supports and permits it, then retry once if granted. If permission is denied or unavailable, or the retry fails, it reports the error and stops. Prompt wording and a skill's compatibility field describe requirements; they don't grant access.

## Skills.

If your agent loads skills from a folder, copy [`skills/automatica11y`](https://github.com/thedannywahl/automatica11y/tree/main/skills/automatica11y) into it. That's one small file, `SKILL.md`. It advertises the tool to the agent, and sends it to `guide skill`. It names no version, so it doesn't go stale. The full steps are the [`automatica11y-runner`](https://github.com/thedannywahl/automatica11y/tree/main/skills/automatica11y-runner) skill, which ships in the package and is what `guide skill` prints. Copy it too if you want the steps available without the network. They're also on this site as [the agent steps](agent-steps.md), with a page for each reference.

## AGENTS.md.

[`AGENTS.md`](https://github.com/thedannywahl/automatica11y/blob/main/AGENTS.md) is for agents that read it but don't load skills. It points to the same steps, and tells contributors how to run and change the code.

## Version safety.

The steps name the version series they were written for, and the first thing they do is check it. If the installed tool is the wrong series, the agent stops and says so, instead of running steps that don't match. An installed copy can be older than the steps expect. In that case use `npx`, which always fetches the latest.

---

---
url: /agent-steps.md
---
# automatica11y runner

This skill turns a request into an `automatica11y` command, runs it, and writes a report from the results. The tool does the testing. This skill never guesses at results.

It's plain Markdown, and it isn't tied to one agent. It needs an agent that can run shell commands (including `npx`) and read and write files.

## Read only what the request needs

This file has what every run needs. The steps for particular cases are in references, so they don't fill your context when the request doesn't need them. When a row below applies, read that whole reference before you act on that part of the request. Paths such as `references/setup.md` are relative to this file. If you can't open the file, print it with the guide command in the last column, using the same command prefix that passed the version check. If neither works, say which reference you couldn't read and stop that part of the work; don't continue from memory.

| When | Read | Or print it with |
|---|---|---|
| `doctor --json` reports a `state` other than `ok`, or the user already said yes to downloading Chromium | `references/setup.md` | `npx --yes --prefer-online automatica11y@latest guide setup` |
| A target is anything other than one live URL: a local page or folder, a Storybook, an npm package (including sub-paths, local builds, plain HTML, and several packages in one target), or a comparison whose targets need grouping | `references/targets.md` | `npx --yes --prefer-online automatica11y@latest guide targets` |
| The user asks to crawl a site, supplies a sitemap, sets discovery limits, or needs authenticated discovery | `references/site.md` | `npx --yes --prefer-online automatica11y@latest guide site` |
| An npm target needs a fixture: after the first run, an archetype the user cares about is `needs-fixture`, or a generated fixture looks wrong | `references/fixtures.md` | `npx --yes --prefer-online automatica11y@latest guide fixtures` |
| Before you write any report or summary of results, every time | `references/reporting.md` | `npx --yes --prefer-online automatica11y@latest guide reporting` |

## What results may claim

The tool is **not** an attestation or certification tool. Automated checks cover only part of WCAG. Never say a target is "accessible" or "compliant," and don't use those words or "passes WCAG" about a target even in a negative or hedged sentence ("I can't say whether the page is accessible"). Say what the results do and don't establish instead. If the user asks whether a target is accessible, open with exactly "Automated checks can't answer that." (ending at "that", never "can't answer whether…") followed by the caveat, then report what the engines found. Don't restate the question anywhere in the reply. For axe-core, say "no automated violations found" when it reports zero violations for a target it tested; otherwise list its violations as reported, and where no page was tested, say so without using that phrase. For IBM Equal Access, report what it found, including when it found no violations, without using that phrase.

For the caveat, write "These automated results do not establish that the page meets WCAG; manual review is still needed." Don't quote a positive accessibility claim just to disclaim it. Use this caveat rather than drawing an overall verdict from automated results, whether positive or negative.

## 1. Check the version

Do sections 1 and 2 before you run an audit. A question to the user about a missing target or an unsupported setting (section 3) can come before or after them. Run this section's version check in its own shell call and read its output and exit code before issuing any `doctor`, `audit`, or `compare` command. Never batch the version check with those commands or run them in parallel. If section 3 says not to run anything until the user answers, ask first and wait; otherwise, a clarification question does not replace the version check.

If the user only wants a report from existing results and says not to rerun the tool, skip sections 1 and 2 and go to sections 5 and 6 to read those files. The version check gates commands, not historical results. Preserve the recorded run date and versions, even when they differ from this skill's series; don't relabel them or require a new audit.

If the user asks only to see a command, such as the version check, and says not to run anything, show it exactly as written in this file, in a code block, and stop.

This skill works with automatica11y **0.12.x**. Run:

```bash
npx --yes --prefer-online automatica11y@latest --version
```

If the command exits with an error or prints nothing, report its exact error text (or say it printed nothing) and the series this copy expects (`0.12.x`), then end the turn. If the output doesn't start with `0.12.`, report the exact version and expected series above, then end the turn. In either case, do not run `doctor` or an audit. If this copy came from a file, offer to read the matching steps with `npx --yes --prefer-online automatica11y@latest guide skill`, but wait for the user's confirmation before running it.

If the user installed the tool globally (`npm i -g automatica11y`), `automatica11y` is on the `PATH` (so is the short name `a11y`), and it runs the same commands as `npx --yes --prefer-online automatica11y@latest`. Every command in this skill is written with `npx`, so replace that prefix with `automatica11y` only when `automatica11y --version` passes the check above. If the installed version is the wrong series, or nothing is installed, use `npx`.

## 2. Check the setup

If the user has already said yes to downloading Chromium, run this instead of the command below, once, and don't run plain `doctor` first:

```bash
npx --yes --prefer-online automatica11y@latest doctor --install-browser --json
```

Apply the exit-code and output checks below, then read `references/setup.md` and follow the row for the state it reports. Otherwise, run:

```bash
npx --yes --prefer-online automatica11y@latest doctor --json
```

For either `doctor` command, if it exits with any code other than 0 or 3, or its output is not a JSON object with a `state` field, report the exact error text (or the invalid output if there is no error text) and exit code, do not run `audit` or `compare`, and end the turn. Otherwise, read its `state`. If it's `ok` (exit code 0), continue. For any other state (exit code 3), read `references/setup.md` and follow the row for that state.

Don't install or configure anything yourself, try other installers, change network settings, or bypass sandbox restrictions. That logic lives in the tool. If the user asked to see the audit command without running it, keep that request in effect after the user chooses to install Chromium in section 2, and show the audit command without running it.

## 3. Turn the request into a command

Only two commands run audits:

```bash
npx --yes --prefer-online automatica11y@latest audit <target> [options]
npx --yes --prefer-online automatica11y@latest compare <target> <target> [<target>...] [options]
```

Use `audit` for one target. Use `compare` when the request names two or more separate targets (each a separate URL, local page or folder, Storybook, or npm package), even when they're different kinds. Pages discovered within one site, and packages grouped into one target, count as one target and use `audit`. A target is `[label=]<spec>`. The label is optional and names the target in the report. A live page's spec is its URL, such as `https://example.com/page`. For every other kind of target, read `references/targets.md` before you build the command. Always write an npm package with the `npm:` prefix.

Options the tool supports (crawl and discovery options are in `references/site.md`):

| Option | Default | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `--wcag 2.0\|2.1\|2.2` | `2.2` | The user names a WCAG version. |
| `--level A\|AA\|AAA` | `AA` | The user names a level. IBM Equal Access has no AAA rules, so it runs its AA rules and says so. |
| `--engine axe,ibm` | both | The user wants one rule engine. |
| `--tiers rules,interactions,computed,conditions,vsr` | all five | The user wants fewer checks. |
| `--screenshots` / `--no-screenshots` | off | Follow checklist step 4 below. |
| `--allow-old-browser` | off | The user explicitly agrees to use the outdated browser reported by `doctor`, including after a failed Chromium download. |
| `--archetypes a,b` | all | The user cares about some components. Choose from button, link, dialog, menu, tabs, combobox, form-field, accordion, tooltip, live-region, chart. |
| `--lib-a11y on,off` | both | Only for libraries with opt-in accessibility features. |
| `--mapping <file>` | none | You wrote or edited a mapping file. |
| `--no-generate` | off | The user wants only authored fixtures and the `button` and `link` templates, with no generated ones. |
| `--max-stories <n>` | 200 | A large Storybook. |
| `--local-package <name=path>` | none | The user points at a local package folder or a packed `.tgz`. Repeat it for each such package. |
| `--out <dir>` | `./a11y-report/<unique-run>` | The user names a folder; use that folder directly. |
| `--plan` | off | You want to see how targets classify without running anything. |
| `--fail-on-axe <impact>` | off | CI-style gating on axe impact (`minor`, `moderate`, `serious`, `critical`). |
| `--fail-on-ibm <1\|2\|3>` | off | Gating on IBM Toolkit level. |
| `--fail-mode any\|all` | `any` | How to combine the two fail flags. |

Examples: `--fail-on-axe serious`, `--fail-on-ibm 1 --fail-mode all`, `--no-generate`, `--plan`, `--wcag 2.1`, and `--level AAA`.

Use this ordered checklist to decide whether to ask or run:

1. If the target is missing or ambiguous, ask for clarification. If the user doesn't name a target to test (a URL, a Storybook, a local page or site, or an npm package), ask for one; don't pick a target for them.
2. If grouping is unresolved for multi-package targets, show the proposed grouping and ask the user to confirm it.
3. If a setting is unsupported, identify it, list supported values, and ask which to use.
4. Handle screenshots as follows:
   1. If the user mentions screenshots, images, or a visual record of results without explicitly requesting annotated screenshots or declining screenshots, ask whether they want annotated screenshots and run nothing until they answer.
   2. Until they answer, show no command containing `--screenshots`, including conditional commands ("if yes, the command is…").
   3. Use `--screenshots` only when the user explicitly requests annotated screenshots of rule violations. If they say no or don't request them, run without `--screenshots`; use `--no-screenshots` when they disable screenshots configured in YAML.

Ask at most one combined question per turn, listing every unresolved item from steps 1–4 in that message. If none apply, run. Preserve any screenshot links from `report.md` next to the findings they support.

Pass only the options in the tables in this skill and its references, with the values they list. If the user names a setting the tool doesn't have, or a value outside those lists (for example, WCAG 3.0), tell them which setting is unsupported, list the supported values, and ask which to use. Don't substitute a default or invent a value.

Show the user the exact command before you run it. If the user only asks to see the command or says not to run it, show the command and stop. When you show a command, don't list or suggest options the user didn't name (no "tell me if you want `--wcag 2.1`…"); state the defaults it uses in plain words instead. If you have questions (a target that could mean two things, a missing target, an unsupported setting), ask them together in one message. Until the user answers every question about the target, grouping, or unsupported settings, don't run `audit` or `compare`; wait for their reply. When you ask to confirm a grouping, show the command for the proposed grouping with the table.

Don't set the fail flags unless the user asks for gating. They change the exit code. They don't change the results.

## 4. npm packages need fixtures

A package's components can't be guessed from its name alone. Run the audit once first: it installs the package, finds its components, writes `<out>/mapping.json`, and fills what it can from templates and generated fixtures. Then, if an archetype the user cares about is marked `needs-fixture`, or a generated fixture looks wrong for the library, read `references/fixtures.md`, write the fixture it describes, and run the same command again. Don't write fixtures before the first run, and don't invent fixtures for archetypes the user didn't ask about. A gap is an honest result. If the user asked for a comparison, give every target the same archetypes.

## 5. Run, then read the results

Run the command. Note the exit code:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | The run completed. Findings don't change this unless a fail flag was set. A target that failed while others ran still exits 0, and the failure is in the results. |
| 1 | The run completed and a fail flag tripped. |
| 2 | The command was wrong. Read the message, fix it, and run again. |
| 3 | An environment problem. Relay the fix. |
| 4 | No target was audited successfully. Read the failed targets and their reasons from `results.json`. |

Then read `<out>/results.json`. It's the source for everything you write. Read `<out>/report.md` too. It's a complete report the tool wrote on its own.

Without `--out`, each invocation uses a unique timestamped folder under `./a11y-report` in the working folder. Read `results.json` and `report.md` from the exact paths printed by that command; its `plan.json`, screenshots, and other artifacts stay in the same run folder. Do not select a different run's report. An explicit `--out` folder is used directly. A normal audit or comparison writes both files even when every target fails during resolution (exit code 4). Those targets are failed, not audited: their reasons are recorded without engine findings or passes. `--plan` writes only `plan.json` and never audit results. The tool writes these artifacts, not the agent. If an expected file is missing, report that gap and the command's error output; don't invent or create replacement results.

A target that can't be reached or built is recorded as failed, with a reason. Don't retry with guesses or substitute a different target. If an npm target failed with a network or install error (for example `ETARGET`), you may run the same command once more. If it fails again, report it. If every target failed (exit code 4), stop and report each failed target and its reason. If others ran, report them, and list the failed target as a gap in coverage.

## 6. Write the report

Read `references/reporting.md` before you write any report or summary, even a short one. Its rules aren't repeated here. These hold in every case:

* Write only from `results.json` and `report.md`. Never write from memory, and never repeat a number you didn't read.
* Report axe-core and IBM Equal Access separately. Never add their counts together or convert one engine's scale into the other's.
* A gap, an error, a not-testable result, or a failed target is a finding. It never counts as a pass.
* Use the caveat sentence above verbatim, and avoid positive accessibility verdicts in headings and summaries.

Always end the turn with a final message listing the report path, results path, and any fixture written. For each generated fixture, include its archetype, exact recipe from `results.json`, lower-evidence caveat, and exact IDs of failed interaction checks in that message, not only in a report file. When the user asks you to write up a report, put the full report, following every rule in `references/reporting.md`, in that final message. Saving a copy to a file is optional and never replaces it. Any shorter summary keeps the run date, the statement that results are a snapshot, any outdated-browser warning, and each WCAG criterion's number and name exactly as `report.md` prints them (for example, 1.1.1 Non-text Content). If a step cannot finish, say so and identify the remaining gaps. If an artifact was not written, say that instead of claiming it exists. For a resolution failure, report the failed target and reason from the results, never a clean audit verdict.

## 7. Stay out of setup

Anything about installing, configuring, or repairing tools belongs to the tool. If `doctor` doesn't cover it, tell the user what failed and stop.

url: /agent-setup.md

# Fixing the setup

Read this when `doctor --json` reports a `state` other than `ok`, or when the user has already said yes to downloading Chromium. The tool decides the state. Don't work it out from prose, and don't install or configure anything the steps below don't name.

## If the user already said yes to downloading Chromium

Complete the version check, then skip the plain `doctor` command and run exactly `npx --yes --prefer-online automatica11y@latest doctor --install-browser --json` once in the shell. Do not substitute `automatica11y` for `npx` for this command. Report its `state` and any `install.output` or `problems`. Don't run `doctor` first, invoke a standalone browser installer, or install anything else. Then follow the row for the new state below.

Browser consent only authorizes the chosen setup step. Preserve any instruction to show the audit command without running it, including after a download or fallback choice.

## What each state means

Exit code 3 means an environment problem. Relay each entry in `problems` (its `message` and `fix`) in plain words, then follow the matching state. When a `fix` names a separate installer, such as `npx playwright-core install`, don't run it; the download below is the only install this skill runs.

| `state` | Next action |
|---|---|
| `ok` | Continue. |
| `node-unsupported` | Node is older than 22. Relay the problem and the fix, then stop until the user applies it. |
| `browser-missing` | Ask only whether to download Chromium. If declined, report that no browser is available and stop. If accepted, run `npx --yes --prefer-online automatica11y@latest doctor --install-browser --json` once and report its result. |
| `browser-outdated` | Follow the ordered browser-choice steps below. The browser is more than two major versions behind Playwright's browser; `browser.kind` and `browser.version` name it. |
| `install-failed-no-browser` | Report the exact error from `install.output`, say that no browser is available, and stop without auditing. |
| `install-failed-outdated` | Report the exact error from `install.output` and name the remaining browser and its version. Call it the outdated browser in every mention, including next to the final command. Use `--allow-old-browser` only if the user already explicitly authorized using that browser; otherwise, explain that its results may be unreliable, ask whether to use it, and wait. If the user declines, say that no current browser is available and use of the outdated browser was declined. State that the audit did not run and no results, report, or screenshots were produced, then stop in that turn without asking again. |
| `other` | Relay the exact problem and fix, then stop until the user applies it. |

A download that succeeds reports `ok`. Continue.

## An outdated browser

1. Name the browser and its version. Explain that results may be unreliable and the report header will flag it.
2. Ask whether to use that browser or download current Chromium through Playwright (about 100 MB), then wait without auditing or downloading.
3. If the user declines both, report that no current browser is available and that use of the outdated browser was declined, then stop without auditing. If their reply answers neither option, ask for clarification and wait.
4. If the user chooses the outdated browser, use `--allow-old-browser` on the audit or comparison and every rerun. Whenever you mention that browser afterward, including next to the final command, use the word "outdated" (for example "the outdated headless-shell 141").
5. If the user chooses a download, run `npx --yes --prefer-online automatica11y@latest doctor --install-browser --json` once and report its result. Follow the row for the new state above. A failed download with an outdated browser remaining (`install-failed-outdated`) requires a separate fallback question unless the user already explicitly authorized that browser.

Download consent never implies outdated-browser consent. The outdated-browser option bypasses only its version check, never missing browsers, unsupported Node, launch failures, or failed rule-engine self-tests.

Add `--allow-old-browser` only after explicit consent to use the outdated browser. Never add it by default.

Do not try other installers, change network settings, or bypass sandbox restrictions.

url: /agent-targets.md

# Writing targets

Read this when a target is anything other than one live URL: a local page or folder, a Storybook, an npm package, or a comparison whose targets need grouping. A target is `[label=]<spec>`. The label is optional and names the target in the report.

## Specs

| The user means | The spec is |
|---|---|
| A live page | `https://example.com/page` |
| A local page or site | `./page.html` or `./dist`. A path with no prefix is relative to the working folder. |
| A Storybook | its URL, or a local folder with `index.json` |
| An npm package | `npm:name`, `npm:@scope/name`, or `npm:name@version`. To test one entry of a package, add a sub-path after the version: `npm:@scope/pkg/button` or `npm:@scope/pkg@1.2.3/button/v2`. The sub-path is what a person would import (`import ... from "@scope/pkg/button"`), and it has to be something the package exports. |
| A local build or packed `.tgz` of a package | `npm:<name>` with `--local-package <name>=<path>`. The name is the `name` in the package's `package.json`. Add one `--local-package` for each package in the target that comes from disk. |

If a local folder is given as a Storybook but has no `index.json`, ask the user for its URL or for a different target before running anything.

If a word could mean a package or a folder, ask the user which one and do not run anything until they answer. Otherwise, use the path rule: A bare word such as `button` is a path: the folder or file `./button`. Always write an npm package with the `npm:` prefix.

## Local packages

For a local packed package, read any README the user supplies and keep `--local-package <name>=<path>` on the initial audit and every rerun. Audit first, then use the documented props to write only requested fixtures marked `needs-fixture` (the fixtures guide has the steps). For React, write `fixtures/<target id>/<archetype>.jsx`, not `.html`, and rerun the same command.

## Plain HTML libraries

A library with no framework, such as a stylesheet package and a script package, is tested by naming the files the page should load as sub-paths: `npm:pkg/base.css,pkg/components.css,other/behavior.iife.js`. A sub-path ending in `.css` is a stylesheet, and one ending in `.js` or `.mjs` is a script. Read the package's documentation or its `exports` to find the right files, and ask the user which stylesheets and scripts they use when the documentation doesn't say. Nothing is generated for plain HTML. Button, link, form-field, dialog, accordion, live-region, menu, and tooltip have templates of bare native markup, so they run with no fixture, and the report says what that does and doesn't show. Say so plainly: a pass on a native template never means the package's own components pass. Tabs, combobox, and chart need a fixture (`fixtures/<id>/<archetype>.html`) or they're gaps. To test the package's own components, write a fixture from its documentation.

## One target can be several packages

Some libraries ship in pieces, such as a stylesheet package and a script package. Join them with commas and no spaces: `npm:@scope/components,@scope/interactions`. They install into one folder and are tested as one target. The first is the primary: it names the target and decides the framework. Every other package is a companion. Each entry can have its own version and sub-path (`npm:a@1.2,b/button`). A list with a space, an empty entry, or the same package twice is rejected. Targets themselves are separated by spaces.

## Reading a comparison in plain language

People write "compare A, B and C and D." Work out the targets before you build the command:

* In plain language, commas can suggest companion packages, and the words "and", "vs", "versus", "against", and "compared with" can suggest separate targets. These are clues for a proposed grouping, not confirmation of it. For "compare A, B and C and D", one proposal is three targets: `A,B`, `C`, and `D`; ask the user to confirm it as described below.
* Give each target a short label that says what it is, such as `pantoken-html=npm:A,B instui=npm:C pantoken-wc=npm:D`. Use the framework or the library's own name, so the report reads clearly.
* Packages from the same organization are separate targets when they're alternatives for the same job (a React build and a web component build of one design system). They belong in one target only when the user says they work together, or when one package is the stylesheet or script half of the other.
* Treat package and target grouping as clear only when the user's words explicitly establish which packages work together and which are alternatives. A comma list, package names, or organization names alone don't establish that.
* Whenever multiple packages could be grouped in more than one way, show your best grouping in a short table of label, packages, and role, and ask the user to confirm it before running. Don't decide the grouping is obvious from names or punctuation. Ask this with any other needed questions in one message.
* Run the same archetypes on every target in a comparison. Say in the report which targets are made of several packages.
* Use `compare` for independent targets even when they're different kinds, such as a live page and an npm package. The comparison report opens with a warning that the evidence isn't equivalent.

url: /agent-site-discovery.md

# Discovering a site

Read this when the user asks to crawl a site, supplies a sitemap, sets discovery limits, or needs authenticated discovery. Only crawl when requested. Preserve the supplied root, sitemap URLs and limits:

```bash
npx --yes --prefer-online automatica11y@latest audit https://example.com/docs/ --crawl
npx --yes --prefer-online automatica11y@latest audit https://example.com/docs/ --sitemap https://example.com/sitemap.xml --crawl
```

Pages discovered within a single site are one audit, not a comparison. Discovery requires one HTTP(S) root. Do not turn discovered pages into `compare` arguments or generate npm fixtures for them. Crawling never means every application state or page was tested.

## Options

| Option | Default | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `--crawl` | off | The user requests crawling a site. |
| `--sitemap <url>` | none | The user supplies a sitemap URL. Repeat for each sitemap; it must share the root's exact origin. |
| `--max-pages <n>` | `100` | The user sets a maximum number of handled requests during discovery (Crawlee handled-request limit; retries are extra). |
| `--max-depth <n>` | `5` | The user sets a maximum discovery depth; seeds are depth 0. |
| `--crawl-delay <seconds>` | `1` | The user sets a crawl delay. |
| `--discovery-scope subtree\|origin` | `subtree` | The user requests origin-wide discovery. |
| `--ignore-robots` | off | The user explicitly requests ignoring robots rules. Robots rules are respected otherwise. |
| `--crawler-config <trusted-local-module>` | none | The user provides a reviewed module for authenticated discovery. |

## Authentication

Authentication uses `--crawler-config <trusted-local-module>`, not inline credentials. Reuse the user's reviewed module; never request tokens, passwords or storage-state contents in chat. If authentication is requested without a module, ask for a trusted module path before auditing. It supplies native Crawlee navigation/Browser Pool hooks plus shared `contextOptions`, `setupContext(context)` and mandatory `verifyPage(page)` for secondary audit contexts. The verifier must reject login/expired pages even with HTTP 200. Hooks can refresh login within at most two request retries; they must not implement unbounded loops. External identity-provider origins require explicit `loginOrigins`; they are not audited. Private sitemaps require cookies configured before fetching or `sitemapHeaders(url)`; localStorage tokens are not automatically HTTP headers. Never run untrusted hook code with secrets or invent a login flow. Link the site's authenticated-discovery documentation when setup help is needed.

For a user-requested crawl capped at 20 pages and depth 2, with a supplied reviewed module at `./crawler.config.mjs`:

```bash
npx --yes --prefer-online automatica11y@latest audit https://example.com/docs/ --crawl --max-pages 20 --max-depth 2 --crawler-config ./crawler.config.mjs
```

Reports and screenshots from authenticated pages may contain sensitive content; avoid copying private data into chat.

---

---
url: /agent-reporting.md
---
# Writing the report

Read this before you write any report or summary of results, every time. Write the narrative from `<out>/results.json`. Never write from memory, and never repeat a number you didn't read. Read `<out>/report.md` too: it's a complete report the tool wrote, and its structure is the one to follow.

## Before you write

Check that the report uses measured wording from the results; names every failed target with its recorded reason; identifies generated-fixture results as lower evidence and names each recipe; and treats every not-testable result, error, or gap as a finding, never as clean coverage.

Use the caveat sentence verbatim: "These automated results do not establish that the page meets WCAG; manual review is still needed." Avoid positive accessibility verdicts in headings and summaries. Quoted rule text is not itself a claim that a target passed; distinguish quotations and negated statements from an actual verdict.

A title, run metadata, and settings may precede the coverage matrix; the matrix comes before the findings. When IBM Equal Access reports no violations but reports needs-review items, write "IBM Equal Access reported no violations in this run" and list the needs-review items in their own section. Do not use "no automated violations found" for IBM. Never say an engine "found nothing" when it reported needs-review items.

## The rules

1. Put the run date and tool versions first. Say that results are a snapshot. When `results.json` contains an outdated-browser warning, keep it in the report header before coverage and findings, name the browser version, and say results may be unreliable. Preserve that warning in any separate summary; do not hide it in a footer or describe the browser as supported.
2. For a comparison, say that every target used the same archetypes, WCAG version, level, and rules, in those words. The settings apply to every target, including one that failed, so don't narrow the sentence to the targets that ran.
3. Open with the coverage matrix (target by archetype by tier). Then give the findings.
4. Keep violations, needs-review items, and passes in separate lists. Never merge them. For each engine and archetype, write three labeled lists (**Violations**, **Needs review**, **Passes**), even when one is just "none". Don't put two of them in one bullet, line, or sentence, even when they're short. For example:

   ```markdown
   **axe-core 4.14.0**
   - Violations: no automated violations found.
   - Needs review: none.
   - Passes: 9 rules.
   ```

   Report only what the results contain; don't add explanations of why something happened.
5. Break findings out by archetype. Within an archetype, order axe-core findings by impact and IBM findings by Toolkit level.
6. Use "no automated violations found" only for axe-core when it reports zero violations for that target; otherwise list its violations as reported. Where it doesn't apply (a failed target, a page that wasn't reached, an engine that didn't run), don't write the phrase at all, not even to say it doesn't apply. Say what's missing instead, such as "axe-core has no results, because no page was audited." For IBM Equal Access, write "IBM Equal Access reported no violations in this run." when it reports zero. Never use "no automated violations found" for IBM. `report.md` writes "No automated violations found by IBM Equal Access." for that case; in your report, write "IBM Equal Access reported no violations in this run." instead, and don't quote or mention the original line. Never say "accessible," "compliant," or "passes WCAG." That includes negative or hedged sentences such as "I can't say whether it's accessible" or "the report doesn't say the site is accessible."
7. Don't print a single score, and don't write an overall or combined line that adds counts across archetypes, fixtures, or engines. Each count stays with its own archetype and engine. If `results.json` or `report.md` has run-level counts across fixtures, don't copy them. If someone insists, pair any number with the coverage matrix and the automated-coverage caveat.
8. Label virtual screen reader output **simulated**. Label library accessibility options **on** or **off** on every result that has one.
9. Treat a gap, a not-testable result, an error, or a failed target as a finding. It never counts as a pass.
10. If the comparison mixes npm package or Storybook targets with live URL or local page or site targets, open the report with a warning that the evidence isn't equivalent.
11. Label every rule finding with its engine. Report axe-core and IBM Equal Access separately. Never add their counts together. Impact is axe-core's own label. IBM Toolkit level is IBM's staged adoption scale (1 is essential, high-impact requirements); report IBM's result even when it has zero violations, without saying "no automated violations found." Don't convert one scale into the other.
12. Report computed checks (contrast measured from resolved styles) in their own section. Give the measured ratio next to the ratio the criterion needs, and name the state or the method. Never add them to axe-core or IBM counts. Treat `undetermined` as a gap, never as a pass. When a control has visible text and a pale edge, the result is `not-applicable`, because the text identifies the control. Say that, and leave it for a person to confirm.
13. Report conditions checks (reduced motion, dark mode, more and less contrast, reduced transparency, forced colors, reflow at 320 pixels, text spacing) in their own section, with the numbers from `results.json`. Never add them to axe-core or IBM counts. In the computed checks section, `not-applicable` means the control's visible text identifies it; in the conditions section, `not-applicable` means the page does not use the feature. Always name the section when reporting this value. Don't list an unused feature, such as a dark theme on a page with no dark theme, as a failure or a pass. Say what each check can't see: JavaScript-driven motion, overlapping text, and two-dimensional content that WCAG exempts from reflow.
14. Say which results come from generated fixtures. A generated fixture is a guess about how the library is assembled, so a failure may come from the wiring and not from the library. Call those results lower evidence than an authored fixture, name the recipe from the **Fixture** column, and list each failed interaction check by its exact ID from `results.json`. Label each fixture-backed result as generated or authored, using those words (a fixture the user wrote is "authored"). In the report and the final summary, head a generated result as `<archetype> (generated fixture, recipe <recipe>, lower evidence than an authored fixture)`, for example `Dialog (generated fixture, recipe dialog-compound, lower evidence than an authored fixture)`, and keep its failed check IDs, even when the full report is written to a file. Don't compare a generated result with an authored one as if they were equal, and never add their checks into one total. If the user wants a result to stand on its own, write an authored fixture for it.
15. When you name a WCAG criterion, use the number and name exactly as `report.md` prints them, and keep its "WCAG data" credit to the W3C. Don't write criterion names or levels from memory.
16. End with a plain method note. Say what automated tools can't catch: whether alt text is meaningful, whether link and heading text make sense in context, cognitive load, real focus and reading order in use, and how real screen readers behave. Those need a person.

Quote selectors and rule IDs exactly as `results.json` has them. Keep `report.md` screenshot links attached to their relevant finding or story when writing a separate summary.

## Site results

For a crawled site, report `discovery.statistics` and `discovery.queue` using their native Crawlee meanings, then the per-page findings and `discovery.gaps`/events. Finished/handled requests are not accessibility passes. Queue exhaustion is not whole-site coverage; pending requests, caps, sitemap failures and failed authentication must be disclosed. Never combine axe/IBM counts or claim a failed login page was audited as the intended application. Reports and screenshots from authenticated pages may contain sensitive content; avoid copying private data into chat. When coverage is missing, say what's missing; don't say what the report doesn't claim about the site (not "the report doesn't say the site is accessible").

## When a target can't be tested

Say these things plainly. Don't soften them, and don't fill in a result.

* **Unsupported framework.** The package needs a framework other than React, Vue 3, Angular 22 and newer, Svelte 5 and newer, plain HTML, or web components. Name it, and say which version is unsupported (Vue 2, Svelte 4, or Angular 21, for example). This version covers React, Vue 3, Angular 22 and newer, Svelte 5 and newer, plain HTML, and web components. A Storybook for the library still works, whatever the framework.
* **Not applicable.** The package has no rendering surface, such as a utility library. There's nothing to test.
* **Not testable.** The content is a canvas with no alternative, or sits in a closed shadow root. The rule engines can't see it, so the result is untested, not clean. Under each engine, write "Violations: not testable (coverage gap)" and the reason. Don't write "none" or "none reported" for an engine that tested nothing. The virtual screen reader also can't read open shadow roots.
* **Gap.** The archetype has no usable fixture or no matching export. Say what the archetype needs.
* **Error.** An interaction or computed check couldn't finish. It's untested, not failed.
* **Undetermined.** A computed check found a gradient, an image, or transparency behind the control, so it can't reduce the page to one color. It's untested, not clean.
* **Failed target.** The target can't be reached, isn't a web page, or couldn't be built. The tool records it as failed with a reason. Tell the user which target failed, using the reason from `results.json`, including when every target failed during resolution before auditing. If others ran, report them, and list the failed target as a gap in coverage.

---

---
url: /limits.md
---
# Limits.

* Automated rules find only part of what WCAG covers. They can't judge whether alt text is meaningful, whether link and heading text make sense in context, cognitive load, real focus and reading order in use, or how real screen readers behave. A person has to check those.
* Components are tested in the states a fixture shows. Dialogs, menus, tooltips, and comboboxes run closed and open, and live regions run before and after the message. Other states aren't visited.
* Content on a canvas with no alternative, or inside a closed shadow root, can't be tested, and the report says so. The virtual screen reader can't read inside shadow roots at all.
* Motion driven by JavaScript timers, such as a carousel that animates with `requestAnimationFrame`, isn't visible to the reduced motion check.
* A Svelte library that imports SvelteKit-only modules (`$app/environment` and the like) can't run on its own. The target fails, and the report names the import.
* Vue 2, Svelte 4 and older, Angular older than version 22, and other frameworks report "unsupported framework." Their Storybooks work, because a Storybook renders stories in a page whatever the framework.
* Native screen readers aren't part of this version.
* Results are a snapshot. The tools run at their latest versions, and the report records them.

## Attribution.

automatica11y reads WCAG criterion numbers, names, levels, and versions from the W3C's published JSON, [wcag.json](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/wcag.json). The package ships that file in `src/data/` without changes.

Source: [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/), W3C. The JSON is used under the [terms in the W3C WCAG repository](https://github.com/w3c/wcag/blob/main/11ty/json/README.md): the source is credited with a link, and the content isn't changed. See also the [W3C Document License](https://www.w3.org/copyright/document-license/) and [W3C Intellectual Rights](https://www.w3.org/copyright/intellectual-rights/). The links that reports build to each criterion are added by automatica11y and aren't part of the W3C data.

Every report repeats this credit in its closing section. To refresh the data, run `npm run update-wcag`.

# Page not found
